name: Wei Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Wei. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. It's all confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a timber-frame crew. The wall panels come off a truck already made in a factory, and we stand them up, fix them together, put the floor joists and roof trusses on. Right now it's eight family houses on a field outside a village called Ashby, and we can get a house to roof height in about four days. I'm the junior, so I'm the one on the end of the panel shouting 'left a bit' and fetching the nail gun cartridges.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drove a parcel van for nine years. I could see where that was going, the company was testing routes with self-driving vans, so three years ago I jumped before I was pushed. Did a short carpentry course, and this firm took me on because I was keen and, honestly, cheap. I'm still behind the others on the hand skills. I can't sharpen a chisel to save my life.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the speed, the fact that the factory panels are basically a giant kit. I like the gadgets: the boss trialled a robot surveying station last month and I was the only one who wanted to touch it. I use AI every day, to read drawings, check spans, write my timesheet. What wears me out is the weather and my lack of experience. The old hands can tell a twisted stud by looking, and I need a level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, shame, I was looking forward to the robots. I'd post something like that, half joking. My mates would say they told me so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my plan's a bit slower, not wrong. I'd still use the AI for my paperwork and drawings, I'd just have to get good at the hand skills the old way. Which, fair enough, I need to anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, finish my carpentry qualification, and practise the hand skills I'm bad at. I'd keep doing my weekend drone work, roof inspections for a roofer I know, about a hundred and fifty a job. And keep the savings ticking over, we've got about three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly disappointed, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the drone work. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I bought a drone for fun, then a roofer I met on site asked if I could look at a chimney without him going up a ladder. Now I do two or three a month. It's not big money, but it's mine, and it's the kind of thing that grows if the tech does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still have to learn the hand skills. Which ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sharpening, scribing, cutting a roof by hand when the truss doesn't fit. Gareth, our lead, does it like he's buttering toast. I watch him and take notes on my phone, which he finds hilarious.

S0.say: I'd say it's a shame because I was looking forward to the robots. I'd post that half joking and my mates would say they told me so.
S0.think: It means my plan is a bit slower, not wrong. I'd still use AI for paperwork and drawings, but I'd have to learn the hand skills the old way, which I need to anyway.
S0.do: Keeps going, finishes his carpentry qualification and practises the hand skills he's weak on. Keeps his weekend drone roof inspections at about 150 a job and keeps three months of savings ticking over.
S0.quote: Shame, I was looking forward to the robots.
S0.fieldNote: Wei is unusual in hoping for more technology, not less. He left parcel driving before automation reached him, and that early move shapes his confidence. His drone side job shows he already builds small bets on new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so get on the right side of it. I'd tell the lads on the crew to learn the new kit before the boss buys it. Some would listen, most wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this suits me. I'm not the best with a chisel, but I'm the best on the crew with a tablet. If the job turns into half carpentry, half running machines, I'm suddenly worth more, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the boss to put me on any training for the new surveying station and the panel-lifting kit. I'd learn the software in the evenings, probably with the AI as my teacher. I'd volunteer to be the person who runs the robot on site, so when the firm buys one, it's mine to drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. It's the kind of change I left driving to chase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth, oddly. He's the best carpenter I know, but he hates screens. He's fifty-one. I'd hate to see him lose out to someone like me who's worse with a saw. I'd try to make him the one who checks the robot's work, because he'd spot mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd lose in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the craft, maybe. I came in too late to be a real craftsman anyway. But if the kids on the course now never learn to cut a roof by hand, that's a loss. Somebody should still know how.

S1.say: It's coming, so get on the right side of it. I'd tell the crew to learn the new kit before the boss buys it, though most wouldn't listen.
S1.think: This suits me: I'm not the best with a chisel, but I'm the best on the crew with a tablet. If the job becomes half carpentry, half running machines, I'm worth more, not less.
S1.do: Asks for training on the robot surveying station and panel-lifting kit and learns the software in the evenings using AI. Volunteers to run any robot the firm buys so it becomes his to operate.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, the kind of change he left driving to chase.
S1.quote: I'm not the best with a chisel, but I'm the best on the crew with a tablet.
S1.fieldNote: Slow change plays to Wei's strengths and he knows it. He's thoughtful about his older crew lead, suggesting he become the one who checks the robot's work. He's also aware that craft knowledge could be lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to be messy, and we need the government and the big firms to keep people afloat while it shakes out. I'd say adapt fast, but I'd also say not everyone can, and that's not their fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years is too fast even for me. I'm good at picking up the new stuff, but if the robot can stand the panels, run itself and check its own work, they don't need me to drive it. Being the early adopter only buys you a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop all spending that isn't needed and get savings from three months to five, which means no holiday and selling my second drone. I'd push the drone inspections hard, because the roofer will want them while it's cheaper than scaffolding. And I'd use AI every evening to look for the jobs that pop up around the robots, setup, repair, whatever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Clear pressure, but I'd have moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the two-year version differ from the longer ones for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I can only use what I've already got: the gadgets, the drone, the curiosity. No time to train in anything serious. With five or ten, I'd plan properly. Two is a scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Hannah do about the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hannah's a primary school teacher, so I think her job lasts longer, little kids need people. We'd lean on her salary and cut everything else. If it got bad, we'd ask the bank to drop to interest-only for a while.

S2.say: This will be messy and we need government and big firms to keep people afloat while it shakes out. Adapt fast, but not everyone can, and that's not their fault.
S2.think: Two years is too fast even for me. If the robot can stand panels, run itself and check its own work, they don't need me to drive it, and being an early adopter only buys a year or two.
S2.do: Cuts non-essential spending, sells his second drone and skips the holiday to grow savings from three to five months. Pushes his drone inspection work hard and uses AI each evening to hunt for jobs around the robots.
S2.feel: Anxious under clear pressure, but feeling he still has moves.
S2.quote: Being the early adopter only buys you a year or two.
S2.fieldNote: Even Wei, who loves new technology, sees that a fast arrival cancels his advantage. He leans on his partner's teaching job as the more lasting income. His pragmatism shows in planning to ask the bank for interest-only payments rather than expecting rescue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people to move if they start now. Get the training out there, cheap and fast. I'd say it to the crew and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years is a decent run for me. I could ride the robot wave on site for three years and build the drone work into a proper little business by the end. I'd be forty-eight, but with a skill that's in demand for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd get a proper commercial drone licence and some insurance, maybe five hundred all in. I'd sign up to run the firm's robots. I'd put a bit into a fund each month, maybe shares in the companies making the robots, since if they're taking my job they might as well pay me back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's still the same end. But I'd feel like I was steering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned buying shares in robot companies. Have you done anything like that before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, through an app, about two thousand in a fund. It went up and down. I'm not an expert, I'd ask the AI to explain things and then ask a real person before putting in much. It's more about not being only on the losing side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the drone business once robots do roof inspections too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good question. Probably it shrinks. But in five years I'd have customers who know me. I think people will still want someone they can ring and shout at when the report's wrong. That's me.

S3.say: Five years is enough for people to move if they start now, so get cheap, fast training out there. I'd say it to the crew and online.
S3.think: Five years is a decent run: three years riding the robot wave on site and the drone work built into a small business by the end. I'd be 48, but with a skill in demand for a while.
S3.do: Gets a commercial drone licence and insurance for about 500 in the first year and signs up to run the firm's robots. Puts a bit monthly into a fund that includes shares in robot makers, checking with a real adviser first.
S3.feel: Uneasy about the same end point, but feeling he's steering.
S3.quote: If they're taking my job they might as well pay me back.
S3.fieldNote: Wei's five-year plan mixes riding the wave at work with growing a side business and owning a small stake in the change. He's careful to say he's no expert and would check with a real person. His sense of control is what keeps his mood lower here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time, so nobody should be caught out. Plan, retrain, save. I'd also say the government should be setting up the safety net now, not in year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is two careers for me. A few more years of framing, then a few years running the kit, then something else. I'd be fifty-three and I'd probably have changed jobs twice by then. That's fine, I've done it before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my carpentry ticket, then do a course in robotics maintenance around year two or three, when the colleges start offering it. I'd keep the drone work going and put a bit away each month, savings and the fund. I'd help Ruby pick her subjects with an eye on what's still standing in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is a long runway, and I like having one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years is two careers. Doesn't the end point still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, somewhere. If AI can do almost everything, my last career is also going. But that's true for nearly everyone, so the whole world would have to work out something new. I'd rather be one of the people who stayed useful longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ruby about her choices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn how things work, not just how to use them. Ruby takes apart her toys to see the motors. I'd encourage that. And I'd tell her it's fine to change direction, her dad did at forty.

S4.say: Ten years is loads of time, so nobody should be caught out: plan, retrain, save. The government should set up the safety net now, not in year nine.
S4.think: Ten years is two careers for me: framing, then running the kit, then something else. I'd be 53 and probably have changed jobs twice, which is fine because I've done it before.
S4.do: Finishes his carpentry qualification, then takes a robotics maintenance course around year two or three. Keeps the drone work and monthly saving and investing going, and helps his daughter choose subjects with 2036 in mind.
S4.feel: Calm, glad of a long runway.
S4.quote: Ten years is two careers for me.
S4.fieldNote: For Wei a decade's warning is a comfort, because moving early is his strength. He does admit the end point leaves him with nowhere final to land, but sees that as a problem everyone shares. His advice to his daughter mirrors his own path.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My whole thing is moving early, and in that one there's no early to move in. What would help is cheap, fast courses that actually lead to work, and some breathing room on the mortgage while people switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: How people feel about being cheap. I got this job partly because I was keen and cost less. If robots are the new cheap, everyone becomes the expensive one. That's a weird thing to get your head round.

headlineQuote: If robots are the new cheap, everyone becomes the expensive one.
portrait: Wei Evans is 43 and three years into timber-frame carpentry, having left parcel driving before self-driving vans arrived. He's still behind on hand skills but uses AI every day, runs a small weekend drone inspection side job and was the only one on his crew keen to try the boss's robot surveying station. He's calm through the plateau and the slow change, which play to his strengths, and anxious when AGI is two years away because there's no time to move early. With five or ten years he plans to run robots, grow the drone work, invest a little and change careers again.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his strength is moving early and that picture gives no time to do it.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, fast courses that lead to real work, and breathing room on the mortgage while people switch.
